liver-b1: The liver is covered by Glisson capsule, a thin fibrous connective tissue layer surrounding the organ. Remember: Glisson capsule covers the liver, while Gerota fascia surrounds the kidney.
liver-b2: The middle hepatic vein is the key landmark that separates the right and left lobes functionally. Remember: hepatic veins divide lobes and segments, while portal veins primarily supply them.
liver-b3: The right hepatic vein divides the right lobe into anterior and posterior segments. A good memory tip is that the right hepatic vein marks the right intersegmental fissure.
liver-b4: The right intersegmental fissure contains the right hepatic vein, which separates the anterior and posterior right lobe segments. Remember: hepatic veins run in intersegmental planes.
liver-b5: The main portal vein normally bifurcates into right and left portal veins at the porta hepatis. Remember: main PV first splits right and left; the right branch later divides anterior and posterior.
liver-b6: The ligamentum teres helps separate the medial and lateral segments of the left lobe. Remember: ligamentum teres is the fibrous remnant of the fetal umbilical vein.
liver-b7: The main lobar fissure contains the middle hepatic vein and serves as a landmark between the right and left lobes. Remember: MLF and middle hepatic vein go together.
liver-b8: The middle hepatic vein is not part of the porta hepatis; it drains superiorly toward the IVC. Remember: porta hepatis contains the portal triad structures, not hepatic veins.
liver-b9: Right-sided heart failure causes venous congestion, leading to enlargement of the IVC and hepatic veins. Remember: backup on the right side of the heart distends systemic veins first.
liver-b10: The right portal vein divides into anterior and posterior branches to supply the right lobe. Remember: right PV = anterior/posterior, while left lobe anatomy is medial/lateral.
liver-b11: A normal portal vein diameter should not exceed 13 mm in most adults. Remember: a portal vein over 13 mm raises concern for portal hypertension.
liver-b12: The right lobe is divided into anterior and posterior segments based on internal vascular landmarks. Remember: the right hepatic vein separates these two right lobe segments.
liver-b13: Portal veins have echogenic walls because they are surrounded by fibrous tissue, making them brighter than hepatic veins. Remember: bright walls = portal veins; thin walls = hepatic veins.
liver-b14: The left lobe is divided into medial and lateral segments. Remember: the ligamentum teres and left intersegmental landmarks help identify this left lobe division.
liver-b15: Budd–Chiari syndrome involves hepatic venous outflow obstruction, so the hepatic veins become narrowed or reduced in caliber. Remember: Budd–Chiari is a hepatic vein disorder, not a portal vein problem.
overview-b16: Yolk sac tumor is a malignant germ cell tumor of the testis, especially important in pediatric patients. Remember: it is classically associated with elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP).
overview-b17: Oncocytoma is most commonly a renal mass and is classically considered a benign kidney tumor. Memory tip: think “renal oncocytoma” when you hear a spoke-wheel type kidney lesion.
overview-b18: Paracolic gutters are the peritoneal spaces that run alongside the ascending and descending colon. Key fact: they serve as pathways for the spread of fluid, infection, or blood in the abdomen.
overview-b19: Angiomyolipoma is the kidney tumor made of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and fat. Remember the name breaks it down: angio = vessels, myo = muscle, lipoma = fat.
overview-b20: Pheochromocytoma is not typically classified as a common pediatric malignant mass, unlike hepatoblastoma, neuroblastoma, and nephroblastoma. Key fact: pheochromocytoma arises from the adrenal medulla and is often associated with catecholamine excess.
overview-b21: A teratoma contains tissues derived from all three germ cell layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Memory tip: teratomas may contain mixed elements like hair, teeth, or cartilage.
overview-b22: A hemangioma is a benign tumor composed primarily of blood vessels. Key fact: it is the most common benign liver tumor in adults.
overview-b23: An insulinoma is typically a benign pancreatic islet cell tumor that secretes insulin. Remember: excess insulin can cause hypoglycemia, making symptoms improve after glucose intake.
overview-b24: A granuloma is a localized collection of inflammatory cells, often formed in response to chronic infection or inflammation. Memory tip: think of it as the body “walling off” an irritant.
overview-b25: A hematoma is a focal collection of blood, usually due to hemorrhage or trauma. Key fact: its sonographic appearance changes over time as the blood ages and organizes.
overview-b26: Choriocarcinoma is the malignant testicular tumor composed of trophoblastic cells. Remember: it is an aggressive germ cell tumor often associated with elevated beta-hCG.
overview-b27: Hematocrit is most helpful after recent trauma because it helps assess blood loss and possible hemorrhage. Memory tip: trauma plus falling hematocrit should raise concern for internal bleeding.
overview-b28: A white blood cell count is most useful when evaluating infection because it often rises with inflammatory or infectious processes. Remember: leukocytosis commonly points toward infection.
overview-b29: Gallstones most commonly produce posterior acoustic shadowing because the dense stone strongly attenuates the sound beam. Key fact: clean shadowing behind an echogenic focus is a classic sign of calculi.
overview-b30: Exudate ascites is peritoneal fluid commonly associated with malignancy, infection, or inflammation. Remember: exudative fluid is protein-rich, unlike transudative ascites from portal hypertension or hypoalbuminemia.
gallbladder-b1: Courvoisier gallbladder classically presents as painless jaundice with a palpable enlarged gallbladder, usually from distal biliary obstruction such as pancreatic head carcinoma. Remember: painful jaundice suggests stones; painless jaundice suggests malignancy.
gallbladder-b2: The mucosal layer is the innermost gallbladder wall layer and lines the lumen. Remember the wall layers from inside out: mucosa, fibromuscular, serosa.
gallbladder-b3: The cystic artery most commonly arises from the right hepatic artery within Calot’s triangle. A key memory fact is that this vessel provides the main arterial supply to the gallbladder.
gallbladder-b4: The fibromuscular layer is the middle layer of the gallbladder wall, lying between the mucosa and serosa. Remember the three layers in order: mucosa, fibromuscular, serosa.
gallbladder-b5: The main lobar fissure is a dependable sonographic landmark that leads to the gallbladder neck from the right portal vein. Remember: finding the MLF often helps locate a contracted or difficult gallbladder.
gallbladder-b6: Cholecystokinin stimulates gallbladder contraction after a fatty meal and also relaxes the sphincter of Oddi. Remember: CCK = contracts the gallbladder.
gallbladder-b7: A normal gallbladder wall measures 3 mm or less on ultrasound. Remember that thickening beyond 3 mm raises concern for pathology such as cholecystitis, hepatitis, or CHF.
gallbladder-b8: The cystic artery is the direct arterial blood supply to the gallbladder. Remember: cystic artery feeds the gallbladder, while the cystic duct drains it into the biliary tree.
gallbladder-b9: The serosal layer is the outermost layer of the gallbladder wall. A helpful memory aid is the wall order from lumen outward: mucosa, fibromuscular, serosa.
gallbladder-b10: Hartmann pouch is a focal outpouching of the gallbladder neck and is a common site for stone impaction. Remember: Hartmann pouch = neck, not the fundus.
gallbladder-b11: The cystic duct connects the gallbladder to the biliary tree by joining the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct. Remember: gallbladder empties through the cystic duct.
gallbladder-b12: The junctional fold is a normal fold located at the gallbladder neck where the body transitions into the neck. Remember: neck landmarks include the junctional fold and Hartmann pouch.
gallbladder-b13: Cholelithiasis means gallstones within the gallbladder. Remember the distinction: cholelithiasis = gallbladder stones, while choledocholithiasis = stones in the bile ducts.
gallbladder-b14: A Phrygian cap is the most common normal variant of gallbladder shape, caused by folding of the fundus. Remember: it is a benign variant, not a pathologic septation.
gallbladder-b15: The normal transverse diameter of the gallbladder should not exceed 5 cm. Remember common normal size limits: length up to about 10 cm and transverse diameter up to 5 cm.
overview-b1: Transitional cell carcinoma arises from urothelium, so it is commonly found in the renal pelvis, ureter, and urinary bladder—not the liver. Remember: TCC follows the urinary collecting system lining.
overview-b2: Neuroblastoma is a common malignant childhood tumor that most often originates in the adrenal gland. Key memory aid: pediatric adrenal mass with possible calcifications suggests neuroblastoma.
overview-b3: Pheochromocytoma is classically a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal gland, usually arising from the adrenal medulla. Remember: 'pheo' = adrenal medulla and hypertension.
overview-b4: The pancreas is primarily a retroperitoneal organ, unlike the liver, gallbladder, and spleen, which are intraperitoneal. Memory tip: many abdominal 'big vessels and pancreas' structures are retroperitoneal.
overview-b5: The ovaries are pelvic intraperitoneal structures, not retroperitoneal organs like the kidneys, adrenal glands, and many abdominal lymph nodes. Remember: KAL = kidneys, adrenals, lymph nodes are retroperitoneal.
overview-b6: Hypernephroma is an older term for renal cell carcinoma, the most common primary malignant renal tumor in adults. Key fact: RCC often arises from the renal cortex.
overview-b7: Comet tail artifact is a reverberation artifact produced by multiple closely spaced reflective interfaces, such as tiny gas bubbles. Remember: short, tapering bright echoes = comet tail.
overview-b8: Cholangiocarcinoma means carcinoma of the bile ducts. Memory tip: 'cholangio-' refers to bile vessels/ducts, distinguishing it from hepatocellular carcinoma of liver cells.
overview-b9: Hepatoma refers to a malignant tumor of the liver, commonly synonymous with hepatocellular carcinoma. Remember: in exam language, hepatoma = primary liver malignancy.
overview-b10: Hepatoblastoma is a malignant liver tumor seen in pediatric patients. Key fact: it is the most common primary hepatic malignancy in young children.
overview-b11: Wilms tumor is another name for nephroblastoma, a malignant pediatric renal tumor. Memory aid: 'nephro-' means kidney, so nephroblastoma = kidney tumor of childhood.
overview-b12: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor that is classically associated with the spleen in abdominal imaging review. Remember: 'angio-' points to blood vessels, and the spleen is highly vascular.
overview-b13: A gastrinoma is most commonly a pancreatic islet cell tumor, even though it secretes gastrin. Key memory: gastrinoma is part of the pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor group.
overview-b14: The lesser sac is the peritoneal space posterior to the stomach and liver and anterior to the pancreas. Remember: it is also called the omental bursa.
overview-b15: The liver is an intraperitoneal organ, whereas the left kidney, aorta, and inferior vena cava are retroperitoneal. Memory tip: kidneys and great vessels sit behind the peritoneum.
liver-b16: A Riedel lobe is a normal anatomic variant describing a tongue-like inferior projection of the right hepatic lobe. Remember: Riedel = right lobe extension, whereas the papillary lobe/process relates to the caudate lobe.
liver-b17: The left portal vein divides into medial and lateral branches, supplying the left hepatic lobe segments. Memory aid: left PV = medial/lateral, while the right PV classically divides into anterior/posterior branches.
liver-b18: After birth, the left umbilical vein fibroses to form the ligamentum teres within the falciform ligament. Remember: teres comes from the umbilical vein, while the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.
liver-b19: The papillary process is the inferior extension of the caudate lobe and can sometimes mimic pathology on imaging. Key fact: papillary process belongs to the caudate lobe, not the right lobe like a Riedel lobe.
liver-b20: Fatty infiltration commonly causes elevated liver function tests because hepatocyte injury alters enzyme levels. Sonography often correlates with this by showing a bright, enlarged liver with increased attenuation.
liver-b21: After birth, the ductus venosus closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum. Memory aid: venosus becomes venosum, while the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres.
liver-b22: A diffusely echogenic liver that is difficult to penetrate is classic for fatty liver disease due to fat increasing sound attenuation. Remember the hallmark triad: bright liver, beam attenuation, and poor visualization of deep structures.
liver-b23: Alcoholism is the most common cause of cirrhosis in classic sonography review material because chronic alcohol injury leads to fibrosis and nodular liver change. Think: long-term alcohol use is a major driver of end-stage liver disease.
liver-b24: Pericholecystic fluid is a gallbladder-related finding, not a typical clinical sign of hepatitis. Hepatitis more commonly presents with systemic symptoms such as jaundice, fever, and sometimes chills.
liver-b25: Candidiasis is more common in immunocompromised patients because fungal opportunistic infections readily involve the liver and spleen. Remember: hepatic candidiasis often appears as multiple small lesions in high-risk patients.
liver-b26: Portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and even portal vein thrombosis are recognized sequelae of cirrhosis, but hepatic artery enlargement is not a classic sequela in this context. Think cirrhosis mainly causes portal venous complications and secondary splenic enlargement.
liver-b27: Hepatopetal means blood flow toward the liver, which is the normal direction in the portal venous system. Memory trick: petal points 'to' the liver, while hepatofugal flows away from it.
liver-b28: Metastatic liver disease is the most common liver malignancy overall because the liver frequently receives spread from other primary cancers. Key fact: hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver cancer, but metastases are more common overall.
liver-b29: Hepatic adenoma is strongly associated with oral contraceptive use, especially in women of childbearing age. Remember: adenomas may hemorrhage, which makes this association clinically important.
liver-b30: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with elevated, not reduced, alpha-fetoprotein, so a reduction is the exception. Remember: AFP is a classic tumor marker that may rise in HCC, especially with cirrhosis.
gallbladder-b16: Gangrenous cholecystitis is a severe complication of acute cholecystitis in which ischemia causes wall necrosis and intramural abscess formation. Remember: “gangrenous” means the gallbladder wall is dying.
gallbladder-b17: Malignant ascites is not a typical cause of diffuse gallbladder wall thickening, whereas AIDS and hepatitis can produce systemic or inflammatory wall edema. Remember: diffuse thickening is often from inflammation or systemic disease, not the ascites type listed here.
gallbladder-b18: This statement is false because females, not males, have a higher risk for cholelithiasis. Remember the classic gallstone risk factors: “female, fat, forty, fertile.”
gallbladder-b19: WES stands for Wall-Echo-Shadow and indicates a gallbladder packed with stones so the lumen is not seen. Remember: wall, then stone echo, then clean posterior shadow.
gallbladder-b20: A gallbladder polyp causes a focal intraluminal finding, not diffuse wall thickening. Remember: diffuse thickening is commonly due to systemic or inflammatory processes like hepatitis, CHF, or ascites.
gallbladder-b21: Tumefactive sludge can mimic gallbladder carcinoma because it may appear as a masslike, nonshadowing intraluminal lesion. Remember: sludge often lacks internal vascularity and may slowly move with position changes.
gallbladder-b22: Gas within the gallbladder wall is the hallmark of emphysematous cholecystitis, a serious complication of acute cholecystitis. Remember: emphysematous = air-producing infection in the wall or lumen.
gallbladder-b23: Adenomyomatosis causes focal wall thickening with comet-tail artifact from cholesterol crystals in Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses. Remember: comet-tail artifact strongly points to adenomyomatosis.
gallbladder-b24: Chronic cholecystitis commonly results from repeated or intermittent cystic duct obstruction by gallstones. Remember: chronic disease reflects recurrent irritation rather than a single acute event.
gallbladder-b25: A gallbladder polyp is typically nonmobile and nonshadowing, unlike most stones, which move and cast shadowing. Remember: polyps are attached to the wall.
gallbladder-b26: Murphy sign is focal tenderness over the gallbladder when pressure is applied with the probe. Remember: the sonographic Murphy sign supports acute cholecystitis when the patient hurts right over the gallbladder.
gallbladder-b27: Emphysematous cholecystitis occurs more often in diabetic patients due to gas-forming organisms infecting the gallbladder. Remember: diabetes is a classic risk factor for this dangerous variant.
gallbladder-b28: Adenomyomatosis contains cholesterol crystals in Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses, producing the typical comet-tail artifact. Remember: RAS plus comet-tail equals adenomyomatosis.
gallbladder-b29: The spiral valves of Heister are mucosal folds located in the cystic duct. Remember: Heister helps identify the cystic duct, not the gallbladder neck or fundus.
gallbladder-b30: Courvoisier’s gallbladder is a distended, palpable gallbladder classically associated with malignant distal obstruction, especially a pancreatic head mass. Remember: painless jaundice with a large gallbladder suggests malignancy.
biliary-b1: Biliary atresia is a congenital obliteration or severe narrowing of the bile ducts, causing neonatal obstructive jaundice. Remember: "atresia" means absence or closure of a normal body opening or tube.
biliary-b2: Cholangiocarcinoma is the primary malignancy arising from the bile duct epithelium. Remember: "cholangio-" refers to bile ducts, while gallbladder carcinoma originates in the gallbladder, not the biliary tree.
biliary-b3: The ampulla of Vater is the dilated union where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct merge before entering the duodenum. Remember: the sphincter of Oddi is the muscular valve that surrounds this terminal region.
biliary-b4: Choledocholithiasis means stones within the common bile duct or biliary tree. Remember: "cholelithiasis" is stones in the gallbladder, while "choledocho-" points to the bile duct.
biliary-b5: Jaundice is the yellow discoloration of the skin and sclera caused by elevated bilirubin, often from liver disease or biliary obstruction. Remember: scleral icterus is a classic early visible sign of jaundice.
biliary-b6: A Klatskin tumor is a hilar cholangiocarcinoma located at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts. Remember: "hilar" lesions often cause intrahepatic ductal dilatation upstream.
biliary-b7: Cholangitis is inflammation, usually infection, of the bile ducts. Remember: the suffix "-itis" means inflammation, so cholangitis literally means inflamed bile ducts.
biliary-b8: Mirizzi syndrome occurs when an impacted stone in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck compresses the common hepatic duct, producing pain, fever, and jaundice. Remember: it is an extrinsic compression problem caused by a gallstone.
biliary-b9: Pneumobilia means air within the biliary tree. Remember: "pneumo-" means air, and it is often seen after biliary procedures or with an abnormal biliary-enteric connection.
biliary-b10: The spiral valves of Heister are folds within the cystic duct that help maintain its patency. Remember: think of the cystic duct as the gallbladder’s twisted, valve-lined connection to the biliary tree.
biliary-b11: An obstruction in the distal common hepatic duct blocks drainage from the liver, so the intrahepatic ducts dilate upstream. Remember: structures proximal to the blockage dilate, while distal structures do not.
biliary-b12: The intrahepatic radicles are the smallest, most proximal branches of the biliary tree within the liver. Remember: bile flows from these tiny radicles toward larger extrahepatic ducts.
biliary-b13: The common bile duct is the most distal major portion of the biliary tree before bile enters the duodenum. Remember: distal means farther along the drainage path, closer to the bowel.
biliary-b14: A distal common duct obstruction can back up the entire biliary system, dilating the common bile duct, common hepatic duct, and gallbladder. Remember: the farther distal the blockage, the more proximal structures may enlarge.
biliary-b15: The cystic duct connects the gallbladder to the rest of the biliary tree. Remember: bile enters and exits the gallbladder through the cystic duct, which joins the common hepatic duct.
pancreas-b1: Glucagon is an endocrine hormone made by islet alpha cells, not part of the pancreas’s exocrine secretions. Exocrine pancreas produces digestive enzymes like amylase and lipase plus bicarbonate-rich fluid.
pancreas-b2: The accessory pancreatic duct is the duct of Santorini. Remember: Santorini = accessory duct, while Wirsung = main pancreatic duct.
pancreas-b3: Von Hippel–Lindau disease is associated with pancreatic cysts and other visceral lesions. A helpful memory point: VHL commonly causes cysts and highly vascular tumors in multiple organs.
pancreas-b4: Adenocarcinoma is the most common pancreatic malignancy by far. Most pancreatic cancers arise from the exocrine ductal system, not from islet cells or cystic neoplasms.
pancreas-b5: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma most commonly occurs in the head of the pancreas. This location often causes early biliary obstruction and painless jaundice because of its proximity to the distal common bile duct.
pancreas-b6: Focal pancreatitis most often involves the pancreatic head. This matters on ultrasound because inflammation in the head can mimic a pancreatic head mass.
pancreas-b7: A diffusely hypoechoic pancreas is more typical of acute pancreatitis, not chronic pancreatitis. Chronic pancreatitis more often shows calcifications, ductal dilatation, and sometimes pseudocyst formation.
pancreas-b8: Weight gain is not a classic feature of acute pancreatitis; patients more often have pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Acute pancreatitis typically presents with severe epigastric pain that may radiate to the back.
pancreas-b9: Lipase is more specific than amylase for acute pancreatitis. A useful memory fact: lipase tends to stay elevated longer, making it especially helpful clinically.
pancreas-b10: The lesser sac is a common location for pancreatic pseudocysts because it lies just anterior to the pancreas. Pseudocysts often collect in spaces adjacent to the inflamed gland.
pancreas-b11: Insulinoma is the most common islet cell tumor of the pancreas. It classically causes hypoglycemia from excess insulin production.
pancreas-b12: A Courvoisier gallbladder refers to a distended gallbladder from malignant biliary obstruction, classically due to a pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. Think: painless jaundice plus enlarged gallbladder suggests malignancy, not stones.
pancreas-b13: A gastrinoma produces excess gastrin and is associated with Zollinger–Ellison syndrome. Key memory aid: gastrin drives severe recurrent peptic ulcer disease.
pancreas-b14: The sphincter of Oddi is the muscular valve that regulates bile and pancreatic juice flow into the duodenum. Remember: Oddi is the sphincter; Vater refers to the ampulla.
pancreas-b15: The main pancreatic duct is the duct of Wirsung. A quick distinction: Wirsung = main duct, Santorini = accessory duct.
biliary-b16: The distal common bile duct is the most frequent site of obstruction because stones commonly lodge near the ampulla. Remember: the farther downstream the blockage, the more likely both proximal intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts will dilate.
biliary-b17: Cholangitis is infection/inflammation of the bile ducts and fits fever, leukocytosis, RUQ pain, plus thick-walled dilated ducts with sludge. Think Charcot triad: fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice strongly suggest cholangitis.
biliary-b18: Pneumobilia produces echogenic linear foci within the liver that create ring-down artifact because air is present in the biliary tree. Key memory aid: air rings down, while stones usually shadow.
biliary-b19: Cholangiocarcinoma often causes obstructive symptoms such as pain, weight loss, and pruritus, with ducts that dilate and then abruptly terminate at the mass. An abrupt cutoff of dilated ducts is a classic malignant obstruction pattern.
biliary-b20: A choledochal cyst is a congenital cystic dilatation of the bile duct and can appear as a focal cystic enlargement of the common bile duct in an infant. Remember: choledochal cysts are classically pediatric biliary cystic lesions.
biliary-b21: Pruritus, weight loss, and elevated bilirubin are clinical findings of cholangiocarcinoma, whereas intrahepatic duct dilatation is an imaging finding rather than a clinical symptom. Clinical means what the patient has or labs show, not what ultrasound shows.
biliary-b22: Pneumobilia is associated with biliary-enteric communication or instrumentation, such as gastric surgery or fistula formation, not cholangiopneumonia. Remember: air in bile ducts usually enters from the bowel or procedures.
biliary-b23: A Klatskin tumor is a hilar cholangiocarcinoma arising at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts. Key fact: 'Klatskin' specifically means a bile duct cancer at the hepatic hilum.
biliary-b24: The bile duct wall should not exceed 5 mm; a thicker wall suggests inflammation or other pathology. Memory tip: thickened duct walls plus ductal dilatation raise concern for cholangitis.
biliary-b25: Choledocholithiasis commonly causes jaundice with elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase from biliary obstruction, but elevated blood urea nitrogen reflects renal status, not bile duct stones. Think obstructive pattern: bilirubin and ALP go up.
biliary-b26: With biliary obstruction, the extrahepatic ducts tend to dilate before the intrahepatic ducts. Remember the sequence: downstream ducts enlarge first, then more proximal branches dilate if obstruction persists.
biliary-b27: Choledochal cysts are primarily congenital and much more associated with pediatric patients, making them less plausible as a typical adult cause of CBD obstruction. In adults, think stones, pancreatitis, or pancreatic carcinoma first.
biliary-b28: Acute bacterial, AIDS-related, and Oriental cholangitis are recognized forms, whereas parabolic cholangitis is not a real clinical entity. Memory aid: if it sounds geometric, it is probably not a diagnosis.
biliary-b29: Bilirubin is the yellow bile pigment formed from breakdown of aged red blood cells and processed by the liver. Remember: excess bilirubin leads to jaundice, a key sign in biliary obstruction.
biliary-b30: In older adults and post-cholecystectomy patients, a common bile duct diameter up to 1 cm can be a normal variant. Key fact: mild ductal enlargement after gallbladder removal may be physiologic, not obstructive.
pancreas-b16: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma commonly causes epigastric pain, weight loss, and jaundice; decreased amylase and lipase are not typical associated findings. Remember: pancreatic cancer often obstructs ducts, leading to elevated—not characteristically decreased—enzyme levels.
pancreas-b17: The head of the pancreas lies within the C-loop of the duodenum, making the duodenum the bowel segment that surrounds it. Key memory aid: the duodenum "hugs" the pancreatic head.
pancreas-b18: Acinar cells perform the exocrine function by producing digestive enzymes secreted into the pancreatic ducts. Remember: acinar = enzyme-producing exocrine tissue, while islets handle endocrine hormones.
pancreas-b19: In acute pancreatitis, the pancreas is most often hypoechoic because inflammation and edema decrease its echogenicity. Key fact: swollen, edematous tissue usually looks darker on ultrasound.
pancreas-b20: The pancreatic head receives arterial supply largely through the pancreaticoduodenal branches associated with the gastroduodenal artery. Memory tip: the head sits by the duodenum, so think "gastro-duodenal" for head blood supply.
pancreas-b21: Insulinomas secrete excess insulin, producing symptoms of hypoglycemia such as weakness, confusion, and sweating. Remember: too much insulin drives blood glucose down.
pancreas-b22: Early acute pancreatitis may appear normal sonographically before edema and peripancreatic changes become evident. Key fact: normal ultrasound does not exclude early pancreatitis.
pancreas-b23: Mucinous cystadenocarcinomas are most commonly found in the body and tail of the pancreas. Memory aid: many cystic pancreatic neoplasms favor the distal pancreas.
pancreas-b24: Simultaneous dilation or obstruction of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct is called the double-duct sign. Remember: two enlarged ducts together strongly suggest a pancreatic head or periampullary lesion.
pancreas-b25: Courvoisier gallbladder refers to a palpable enlarged gallbladder caused by distal biliary obstruction, often near the pancreatic head. Key fact: painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder raises concern for malignancy.
pancreas-b26: The pancreas is a retroperitoneal organ, located behind the peritoneal cavity except for a small portion of the tail relation. Memory tip: most of the pancreas lies deep and posterior in the abdomen.
pancreas-b27: The pancreatic head lies to the right of the SMV, anterior to the IVC, and inferior to the portal vein. Remember: the head occupies the right-sided duodenal loop near these major vessels.
pancreas-b28: The splenic vein runs posterior to the pancreas and is an important landmark outlining the tail region. Memory aid: follow the splenic vein behind the gland toward the tail.
pancreas-b29: The pancreatic neck lies directly anterior to the portal confluence, where the SMV and splenic vein join. Key fact: neck = portal confluence landmark.
pancreas-b30: Insulin is the pancreatic hormone that promotes cellular uptake and use of glucose, opposing glucagon's effect on raising blood sugar. Remember: insulin lowers serum glucose by moving it into cells.
spleen-b1: An accessory spleen most often appears as a small, round mass near the splenic hilum with echogenicity identical to the main spleen. Key fact: accessory spleens are a common normal variant and are usually located at the hilum.
spleen-b2: Angiosarcoma is the rare malignant vascular tumor of the spleen. Key fact: think “angio” = vessel, so angiosarcoma is a cancer arising from blood vessel tissue.
spleen-b3: A splenic infarct classically appears as a wedge-shaped, hypoechoic peripheral lesion and fits sudden LUQ pain without trauma. Key fact: infarcts often point toward the hilum because they follow segmental vascular distribution.
spleen-b4: Splenic hemangiomas are most commonly echogenic on ultrasound. Key fact: like many hemangiomas elsewhere, their vascular channels often create a bright appearance.
spleen-b5: Erythropoiesis is the production of red blood cells. Key fact: “erythro-” means red and “-poiesis” means formation.
spleen-b6: The splenic artery courses along the superior border of the pancreatic body and tail. Key fact: on sonography, the tortuous splenic artery is a landmark for the pancreas’ superior aspect.
spleen-b7: Portal hypertension is the most common cause of splenomegaly because increased portal venous pressure leads to congestion of the spleen. Key fact: enlarged spleen commonly accompanies portal-system venous backpressure.
spleen-b8: Red pulp performs the spleen’s phagocytic function by filtering blood and removing old or damaged blood cells. Key fact: red pulp is the blood-filtering portion of the spleen.
spleen-b9: A small, rounded, echogenic, nonshadowing splenic mass is most characteristic of a hemangioma. Key fact: hemangioma is the most common benign primary splenic tumor.
spleen-b10: The spleen is intraperitoneal, meaning it is covered by peritoneum and suspended by peritoneal ligaments. Key fact: the spleen lies within the left upper intraperitoneal compartment.
spleen-b11: White pulp is responsible for the spleen’s lymphatic and immune functions. Key fact: white pulp contains lymphoid tissue surrounding splenic arteries.
spleen-b12: The splenic vein runs along the posterior aspect of the pancreatic body and tail. Key fact: this vessel is an important sonographic landmark behind the pancreas.
spleen-b13: The spleen stores iron, helps defend against disease, and serves as a blood reservoir, but it does not destroy phagocytic cells. Key fact: splenic phagocytic cells remove old blood cells—they are not the target of destruction.
spleen-b14: The splenic hilum is the most common location for an accessory spleen. Key fact: when a small mass matches splenic echogenicity at the hilum, think accessory spleen first.
spleen-b15: Trauma, hemolytic disorders, and mononucleosis can all enlarge the spleen, whereas pancreatitis is not a typical cause of splenomegaly. Key fact: splenomegaly is commonly linked to hematologic, infectious, or portal venous conditions.
urinary-b1: The nephron is the kidney’s functional unit because it filters blood and forms urine. Remember: each kidney contains about 1 million nephrons, made of a glomerulus plus renal tubules.
urinary-b2: The kidneys are retroperitoneal organs, meaning they lie behind the peritoneal lining of the abdomen. Memory tip: think “R” for retroperitoneal and renal—both start with R.
urinary-b3: Gerota fascia is the fibrous protective covering surrounding the kidney and perirenal fat. Key fact: it is also called the renal fascia and helps contain inflammation or hemorrhage around the kidney.
urinary-b4: The left renal vein passes anterior to the aorta and posterior to the SMA, creating the classic “nutcracker” location. This relationship is important because compression here can cause nutcracker syndrome.
urinary-b5: Compensatory hypertrophy is enlargement of the normal kidney when the opposite kidney is absent or poorly functioning. Remember: the healthy kidney “compensates” by increasing in size and workload.
urinary-b6: A dromedary hump is a normal variant that appears as a bulge on the lateral border of the left kidney. Memory aid: it resembles the hump of a dromedary camel.
urinary-b7: A duplicated collecting system is the most common congenital urinary tract anomaly. Key fact: it may involve duplication of the renal pelvis, ureter, or both.
urinary-b8: The pelvis is the most common location for an ectopic kidney because ascent from the fetal pelvis fails during development. Remember: ectopic kidneys usually stay low rather than reaching the upper abdomen.
urinary-b9: Acute renal failure typically raises BUN and creatinine, so decreased levels would not be expected. Remember: oliguria, hypertension, and hematuria are common clinical findings when renal function suddenly declines.
urinary-b10: Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of chronic renal failure because long-term hyperglycemia damages the glomeruli. Memory tip: diabetic nephropathy is a leading cause of end-stage renal disease.
urinary-b11: Chronic renal failure usually makes the kidneys smaller and more echogenic due to scarring and parenchymal loss. Key fact: increased cortical echogenicity often reflects chronic medical renal disease.
urinary-b12: Cortical cysts arise from the renal cortex and often project outward from the kidney surface. Remember: they are the most common simple renal cysts seen on ultrasound.
urinary-b13: von Hippel–Lindau syndrome is associated with CNS and orbital tumors plus renal cysts and adrenal tumors. Key fact: it classically includes hemangioblastomas and an increased risk of renal cell carcinoma.
urinary-b14: Acute tubular necrosis is the most common cause of acute renal failure, usually from ischemia or nephrotoxic injury. Memory tip: ATN is a common intrinsic renal cause after shock, sepsis, or toxic exposure.
urinary-b15: Smooth walls are a feature of a simple cyst, not a complex cyst. Remember: complex cysts show concerning findings such as septations, internal echoes, or mural nodules.
spleen-b16: Diffuse splenic infiltration by lymphoma or leukemia commonly enlarges the spleen, producing splenomegaly. Remember: hematologic malignancies often cause a diffusely enlarged, sometimes homogeneous spleen.
spleen-b17: The splenic artery is one of the three main branches of the celiac trunk. A helpful memory aid is 'celiac gives left gastric, common hepatic, and splenic.'
spleen-b18: Histoplasmosis is a granulomatous disease, so the spleen commonly shows multiple granulomas, often appearing as tiny echogenic calcified foci. Think: fungal infection plus spleen often equals granulomas.
spleen-b19: After blunt abdominal trauma, a complex splenic mass most likely represents a hematoma from hemorrhage. Key point: traumatic splenic hematomas are commonly complex or heterogeneous on ultrasound.
spleen-b20: Sickle cell disease often causes splenic congestion and enlargement early in the disease, leading to splenomegaly. Remember: repeated sickling can later damage the spleen, but enlargement is a classic finding.
spleen-b21: Epstein–Barr virus is a herpesvirus and a classic cause of infectious mononucleosis, especially in children and young adults. Memory tip: mono is strongly associated with splenic enlargement and rupture risk.
spleen-b22: Culling is the splenic process of removing abnormal or aged red blood cells from circulation. Remember: 'culling' means clearing out defective cells, while pitting removes inclusions from otherwise intact cells.
spleen-b23: A splenic infarct is an area of ischemic necrosis caused by interrupted blood flow and lack of oxygen. Key fact: infarcts are often wedge-shaped with the apex pointing toward the hilum.
spleen-b24: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease that can produce granulomas in the spleen and many other organs. Think: noncaseating granulomas throughout the body are classic for sarcoidosis.
spleen-b25: A hydatid cyst results from echinococcal tapeworm infestation and can involve the spleen as a complex cystic lesion. Memory aid: hydatid disease is the classic parasitic cyst to know in abdominal imaging.
spleen-b26: Most splenic hemangiomas are incidental and asymptomatic, so no specific clinical finding is typically present. Remember: hemangioma is the most common benign splenic neoplasm and is often discovered by chance.
spleen-b27: Reed–Sternberg cells are the hallmark pathologic finding of Hodgkin lymphoma. A quick memory tip: 'Reed–Sternberg equals Hodgkin' is a high-yield association.
spleen-b28: This statement is false because the spleen actually has a concave medial/superior border and a convex lateral/inferior surface, not the reverse. Remember the splenic hilum lies along the concave medial aspect.
spleen-b29: The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein. Memory aid: portal vein = SMV + splenic vein.
spleen-b30: Small echogenic foci scattered throughout the spleen most commonly represent benign granulomas, often from prior granulomatous infection. Key fact: healed granulomas frequently calcify and appear bright on ultrasound.
urinary-b16: A hemorrhagic renal cyst contains blood, so hematuria is a likely clinical finding. Remember: bleeding cysts may also cause pain and internal echoes rather than the anechoic appearance of a simple cyst.
urinary-b17: Infantile polycystic kidney disease is another name for autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. Key memory aid: ARPKD typically presents in infancy or childhood, unlike ADPKD which usually presents later.
urinary-b18: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease classically produces bilaterally enlarged, diffusely echogenic kidneys from innumerable tiny cysts. Remember: the cysts are often too small to resolve individually, giving a bright solid-looking appearance.
urinary-b19: Tuberous sclerosis is associated with seizures/epilepsy and multiple hamartomas, including renal angiomyolipomas. Remember the classic triad: seizures, intellectual disability, and facial adenoma sebaceum.
urinary-b20: Simple renal cysts are most often incidental findings and produce no symptoms. Key fact: on ultrasound they are typically anechoic, thin-walled, and show posterior acoustic enhancement.
urinary-b21: A ureteral stricture is an intrinsic cause because the narrowing occurs within the ureter itself, not from outside compression. Remember: pregnancy and uterine leiomyoma are classic extrinsic compressive causes.
urinary-b22: Long-term hemodialysis is associated with acquired renal cystic disease. Key memory point: this develops in chronically diseased kidneys and increases the risk of renal cell carcinoma.
urinary-b23: Pyonephrosis means pus within an obstructed collecting system. Remember: think 'pyo' = pus, and sonographically you may see hydronephrosis with low-level internal echoes or fluid-debris levels.
urinary-b24: Candida albicans is the most common cause of fungal urinary tract infection. Key fact: fungal infections are especially seen in immunocompromised, diabetic, or catheterized patients.
urinary-b25: Hypercalcemia is not a typical clinical finding of glomerulonephritis, whereas proteinuria, azotemia, and recent throat infection can be seen. Remember: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis often follows a throat infection.
urinary-b26: Urethritis is inflammatory and is not a classic intrinsic obstructing lesion causing hydronephrosis. Remember: ureterocele, stones, and UPJ obstruction directly block urine flow within the urinary tract.
urinary-b27: Weight loss is not a typical clinical feature of nephrocalcinosis, while UTIs, urinary calculi, and hyperparathyroidism are associated findings. Remember: nephrocalcinosis reflects calcium deposition in the renal parenchyma.
urinary-b28: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is well known for associated extrarenal cysts, especially in the liver and pancreas. Memory aid: ADPKD is a systemic cystic disorder, not just a kidney disease.
urinary-b29: A staghorn calculus is a large branching stone that fills the renal pelvis and often extends into the calyces. Remember: its shape resembles deer antlers, which explains the name.
urinary-b30: The ureterovesicular junction is the most common site where a stone becomes lodged because it is one of the narrowest points in the ureter. Remember the three narrowing sites: UPJ, crossing iliac vessels, and UVJ.
adrenal-b1: Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism, commonly caused by an adrenal adenoma and associated with hypertension and polydipsia. Thinning arms and legs is more characteristic of Cushing syndrome, which helps distinguish the two adrenal disorders.
adrenal-b2: Hematocrit is useful because internal bleeding lowers the proportion of red blood cells in circulating blood. Remember: hemorrhage often trends with falling hematocrit and hemoglobin values.
adrenal-b3: Cushing syndrome fits the combination of hypertension, hyperglycemia, obesity, and an adrenal mass because it results from excess cortisol. A classic memory clue is central obesity with steroid excess.
adrenal-b4: This is correct because the adrenal glands are endocrine, not exocrine, glands—they secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream. Key fact: adrenal glands have a cortex and medulla and are also called suprarenal glands.
adrenal-b5: Gerota fascia is the renal fascia that encloses the kidneys and adrenal glands within the perirenal space. A good memory tip is that the adrenal sits in the same fascial compartment as the kidney.
adrenal-b6: The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein, whereas the right suprarenal vein drains directly into the IVC. Remember: left adrenal follows the left renal vein, right adrenal goes straight to the IVC.
adrenal-b7: With active internal hemorrhage, hematocrit decreases as blood loss reduces circulating red blood cell volume. Memory aid: ongoing bleeding causes H&H to trend down.
adrenal-b8: Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream, unlike exocrine glands, which use ducts. Think: endocrine equals 'into blood,' exocrine equals 'through a duct.'
adrenal-b9: A hematoma is a localized collection of blood, often due to trauma or hemorrhage. Easy memory fact: 'hema-' means blood, so hematoma literally refers to a blood collection.
adrenal-b10: The adrenal glands receive arterial supply from the suprarenal arteries, typically described as superior, middle, and inferior branches. Remember the glands are highly vascular because they produce and release hormones rapidly.
adrenal-b11: An acute drop in hematocrit suggests bleeding, not a hyperfunctioning adrenal adenoma. Functioning adenomas are linked to hormone excess syndromes like Cushing or Conn, not hemorrhagic lab changes.
adrenal-b12: Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal medulla, not the cortex. Memory tip: cortex makes steroids—cortisol, aldosterone, and androgens—while the medulla makes catecholamines.
adrenal-b13: Norepinephrine is produced by the adrenal medulla, which secretes catecholamines. A helpful fact is that the medulla handles the body’s immediate stress response.
adrenal-b14: Epinephrine and norepinephrine are the catecholamines responsible for the classic 'fight-or-flight' response. Remember: these medullary hormones increase heart rate, blood pressure, and alertness.
adrenal-b15: The right adrenal gland lies posterior and lateral to the IVC, a key landmark during sonography. Memory aid: on the right, look just behind the IVC for the adrenal.
adrenal-b16: An anechoic mass with posterior acoustic enhancement in the adrenal region is most consistent with an adrenal cyst. Remember: simple cysts are classically fluid-filled, echo-free, and enhance posteriorly.
adrenal-b17: The right suprarenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava, unlike the left suprarenal vein, which typically drains into the left renal vein. A quick memory tip: right is short and direct to the IVC.
adrenal-b18: Pheochromocytoma arises from the adrenal medulla and can secrete catecholamines, causing severe hypertension, tachycardia, and tremors. Think 'pheo = pressure' for its classic hypertensive presentation.
adrenal-b19: These findings suggest Cushing syndrome, which can be caused by either an adrenal adenoma or primary adrenal carcinoma. Key clue: truncal obesity with thin extremities points to excess cortisol production.
adrenal-b20: A pheochromocytoma most commonly appears as a hyperechoic adrenal mass on ultrasound. Memory aid: this catecholamine-producing tumor is often a solid, bright-appearing adrenal lesion.
adrenal-b21: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial malignant tumor in children and often arises from the adrenal gland. Remember: pediatric adrenal mass plus malignancy should make you think neuroblastoma first.
adrenal-b22: Neuroblastoma most often appears heterogeneous with calcifications because of necrosis, hemorrhage, and tumor mineralization. A helpful clue is that calcifications are common in this aggressive pediatric adrenal tumor.
adrenal-b23: Neuroblastoma typically presents before age 5, making it a classic early childhood malignancy. Memory tip: if a very young child has an adrenal-region mass, neuroblastoma is high on the list.
adrenal-b24: Aldosterone regulates blood pressure by controlling sodium retention and water balance in the kidneys. Remember: aldosterone from the adrenal cortex helps the body 'hold salt,' which raises volume and pressure.
adrenal-b25: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), secreted by the anterior pituitary, stimulates the adrenal glands to release hormones. Think of ACTH as the pituitary's signal telling the adrenal cortex to get to work.
adrenal-b26: Neuroblastoma is malignant, so it is the exception among these otherwise benign adrenal masses. Key fact: it is a pediatric cancer commonly arising in the adrenal medulla.
adrenal-b27: Pheochromocytoma causes excess catecholamine release, leading to hypertension, sweating, and tremors rather than bradycardia. Remember: catecholamines usually increase heart rate, not slow it.
adrenal-b28: Androgens contribute to the development of male characteristics and are produced in part by the adrenal cortex. Memory aid: adrenal androgens support secondary sex characteristics.
adrenal-b29: The adrenal glands receive blood from superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries, derived from the inferior phrenic arteries, aorta, and renal arteries. The celiac trunk is not a standard source of adrenal arterial supply.
adrenal-b30: Adrenal glands are not easily identified in most adults, so that statement is false. Key fact: they are much easier to visualize in fetuses and neonates because they are relatively larger.
vasculature-b1: Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder classically associated with tall stature and aortic root/valvular insufficiency, especially aortic and mitral valves. Remember: Marfan weakens elastic tissue, so the aorta is a major site of complications.
vasculature-b2: The tunica intima is the innermost vessel layer and lies directly against the blood flow. Think 'intima = internal' to remember it lines the lumen.
vasculature-b3: The celiac artery is the first major unpaired visceral branch arising from the proximal abdominal aorta. A quick sequence to remember is celiac first, then SMA.
vasculature-b4: A mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysm caused by or associated with infection of the vessel wall. Despite the name, 'mycotic' usually refers to infectious, not specifically fungal, aneurysms.
vasculature-b5: The celiac axis classically gives rise to the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries. Remember the 'big three' celiac branches: left gastric, splenic, hepatic.
vasculature-b6: The tunica adventitia is the outermost vessel wall layer, providing support and protection. Think 'adventitia = external covering' around the vessel.
vasculature-b7: After a meal, the superior mesenteric artery supplies the actively digesting small bowel, so it normally shows low-resistance flow. Key memory aid: fed bowel needs more continuous forward perfusion.
vasculature-b8: The superior mesenteric artery is the second major unpaired branch off the abdominal aorta, arising just inferior to the celiac trunk. Remember the order: celiac first, SMA second.
vasculature-b9: The superior mesenteric artery changes its waveform significantly after eating because intestinal demand increases postprandially. In fasting it is higher resistance, but after meals it becomes low resistance.
vasculature-b10: With small bowel ischemia, the SMA fails to show the normal postprandial vasodilation pattern and remains high resistance. Remember: ischemic bowel cannot achieve the expected low-resistance fed state.
vasculature-b11: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is diagnosed when the abdominal aorta measures greater than 3 cm in diameter. A useful cutoff to memorize is 'AAA = aorta above 3.'
vasculature-b12: Budd–Chiari syndrome refers to hepatic venous outflow obstruction due to occlusion of the hepatic veins. Key fact: it causes congested, enlarged liver because blood cannot drain normally.
vasculature-b13: Fusiform aneurysms are the most common form of abdominal aortic aneurysm, involving symmetric dilation of the vessel wall. Think 'fusiform = full circumference' enlargement.
vasculature-b14: The splenic artery can mimic the main pancreatic duct because its tortuous course runs along the superior/posterior pancreas. Color Doppler helps distinguish a vessel from the nonvascular pancreatic duct.
vasculature-b15: The inferior vena cava carries systemic venous blood directly into the right atrium. Remember: all IVC flow returns to the right side of the heart first.
vasculature-b16: The main portal vein is formed by the confluence of the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein, typically posterior to the pancreatic neck. Memory tip: think 'S + SMV = PV.'
vasculature-b17: The hepatic veins drain directly into the IVC just below the diaphragm as they exit the liver. Key fact: they are usually three major veins—right, middle, and left.
vasculature-b18: The aorta arises from the left ventricle and carries oxygenated blood to the systemic circulation. Remember: 'left ventricle launches the body’s main artery.'
vasculature-b19: The hepatic artery supplies the liver continuously, so it normally has a low-resistance waveform with forward diastolic flow. Memory tip: organs needing constant perfusion show low resistance.
vasculature-b20: Neck pain is not a typical finding of an abdominal aortic aneurysm; AAA symptoms more often include back pain, abdominal bruit, or lower extremity ischemic pain. Remember: AAA symptoms stay in the abdomen, back, and legs.
vasculature-b21: A thin echogenic line gently moving within the aneurysm lumen is an intimal flap, which is classic for aortic dissection. Key fact: mural thrombus is adherent to the wall and does not sway freely.
vasculature-b22: The left renal vein courses between the superior mesenteric artery anteriorly and the aorta posteriorly. Memory aid: this is the 'nutcracker' position of the left renal vein.
vasculature-b23: The common iliac artery supplies the lower extremities, so it typically shows a high-resistance peripheral arterial waveform. Remember: limb arteries usually have sharper systolic peaks and less diastolic flow.
vasculature-b24: The left renal vein passes anterior to the left renal artery as it travels toward the IVC. Key fact: the vein is the more anterior structure at the renal hilum on the left.
vasculature-b25: The right renal vein is shortest because the IVC lies on the right side of the spine, close to the right kidney. Memory tip: 'right vein, short trip; left vein, long crossing.'
vasculature-b26: Right-sided heart failure elevates central venous pressure, causing dilation of the IVC and hepatic veins. Remember: venous backup from the right heart shows up in the systemic veins.
vasculature-b27: Hepatic veins normally demonstrate a pulsatile, triphasic waveform because pressure changes from the right atrium are transmitted back to them. Key fact: their flow reflects the cardiac cycle.
vasculature-b28: The IVC should not normally exceed 2.5 cm in diameter; larger size suggests elevated right-sided venous pressure. Memory tip: a plethoric IVC points to impaired right heart drainage.
vasculature-b29: This statement is false because the IVC is a vein, so it does not normally show high-resistance arterial flow. Remember: normal IVC flow is venous, phasic, and affected by respiration.
vasculature-b30: This is not true because most abdominal aortic aneurysms are true aneurysms involving all three vessel wall layers. Key fact: the most common AAA location is infrarenal.
gi-b1: Visceral is not one of the five sonographic gut wall layers; the bowel wall layers include mucosa, muscularis mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, and serosa. Remember: serosa is the outer echogenic layer.
gi-b2: Normal bowel is usually compressible with graded compression, so saying it does not compress is incorrect. A quick memory aid: normal bowel is thin, mobile, and should show some peristalsis.
gi-b3: In pyloric stenosis, the pyloric muscle is abnormally thickened, not less than 8 mm. Remember the classic sonographic signs: transverse 'doughnut' and longitudinal 'cervix' appearance.
gi-b4: Acute appendicitis classically appears as a noncompressible blind-ended tubular structure, so a compressible tube is not typical. Key memory fact: diameter greater than 6 mm supports appendicitis.
gi-b5: Constipation is not a classic clinical finding of acute appendicitis, whereas RLQ pain, rebound tenderness, and leukocytosis are common. Remember: appendicitis often presents with pain plus inflammatory signs.
gi-b6: Pyloric stenosis classically affects first-born males, not first-born females. A helpful clue is the infant with projectile nonbilious vomiting, weight loss, dehydration, and a palpable olive.
gi-b7: Red currant jelly stools are classic for intussusception because of bowel ischemia and sloughed mucosa mixed with blood and mucus. Remember: intussusception is bowel telescoping, often in infants.
gi-b8: Intussusception usually does not mimic pyloric stenosis because it presents with episodic pain and currant jelly stools rather than gastric outlet obstruction. Pylorospasm and GERD are more common pyloric stenosis look-alikes.
gi-b9: Most gastric cancers are adenocarcinomas arising from the glandular epithelium of the stomach. Memory aid: when asked about stomach malignancy, think 'adeno' first.
gi-b10: A trichobezoar is a mass of ingested hair that can obstruct the bowel, especially in pediatric patients. Remember: 'tricho-' means hair, while 'phyto-' refers to plant material.
gi-b11: Crohn disease is an autoimmune inflammatory bowel disease marked by recurrent gastrointestinal inflammation. Key fact: it causes transmural inflammation and can produce skip lesions.
gi-b12: Intussusception is the telescoping of one bowel segment into another. Remember the target or donut sign on transverse ultrasound is a classic clue.
gi-b13: Midgut malrotation is suggested sonographically by an abnormal SMA-SMV relationship, often with the SMV lying left of the SMA. Memory tip: normal anatomy usually places the SMV to the right of the SMA.
gi-b14: Bowel protruding into the groin is an inguinal hernia. Remember: inguinal hernias follow the inguinal canal and are the most common abdominal wall hernias.
gi-b15: A Spigelian hernia occurs through a weakened area along the semilunar line, often in the lower lateral rectus region. Memory aid: think 'Spigelian = side of the rectus.'
gi-b16: McBurney point is the classic site of maximal pain and rebound tenderness in acute appendicitis because it overlies the usual appendix location in the right lower quadrant. Remember: McBurney point = appendicitis landmark.
gi-b17: McBurney point is located about halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the umbilicus on the right. This surface landmark helps localize the base of the appendix during clinical evaluation.
gi-b18: The olive sign refers to a palpable enlarged pyloric sphincter in infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Think of it as a small “olive-shaped” mass felt in the epigastric/right upper abdominal region.
gi-b19: Rebound tenderness is classically associated with appendicitis because peritoneal irritation causes pain when pressure is suddenly released. Key memory aid: rebound pain suggests an acute inflammatory abdominal process, especially appendicitis.
gi-b20: The vermiform appendix most commonly arises from the cecum, just below the ileocecal valve. Remember: appendix = cecal blind-ended tubular structure in the right lower quadrant.
gi-b21: A rectus sheath hematoma involves bleeding into the abdominal wall, so hematocrit tends to decrease, not increase. Risk factors include trauma or strain such as childbirth, coughing, or sneezing.
gi-b22: Crohn disease commonly shows bowel wall thickening, hyperemia, and noncompressible bowel, but not increased peristalsis. A helpful clue is that inflamed bowel often becomes stiff and hypomotile rather than more active.
gi-b23: Vomiting, red currant jelly stools, and leukocytosis are recognized findings with intussusception, but being a first-born male infant is not a typical clinical finding. Remember the classic triad includes pain, vomiting, and bloody stool.
gi-b24: Fluid-filled, distended bowel loops are a classic sonographic sign of intestinal obstruction because fluid backs up proximal to the blockage. Think: dilated loops plus fluid = obstructive pattern.
gi-b25: Traditionally, intussusception is reduced with a contrast enema, which can be both diagnostic and therapeutic. Key fact: the enema may unfold the telescoped bowel without surgery.
gi-b26: Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children younger than 2 years. Remember: telescoping bowel is a leading pediatric emergency in this age group.
gi-b27: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis most often presents between 2 and 8 weeks of age, when progressive pyloric muscle hypertrophy causes gastric outlet obstruction. Think of the typical young infant with nonbilious projectile vomiting.
gi-b28: The right lateral decubitus position helps the stomach fill and can improve visualization of the pylorus during sonography. A full antrum often serves as an acoustic window to the pyloric canal.
gi-b29: Diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis classically include pyloric muscle thickness of 3 mm and channel length of 17 mm. Easy memory aid: '3 and 17' are the key pyloric stenosis numbers.
gi-b30: Crohn disease commonly presents with abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, and weight loss, but a palpable abdominal mass is not a typical clinical finding. Remember: Crohn is an inflammatory bowel disease marked by chronic GI symptoms and weight loss.
chest-b1: Migraine medication use is associated with secondary retroperitoneal fibrosis, especially older ergot-derived drugs. Remember: RPF can be drug-induced and often encases retroperitoneal structures like the ureters.
chest-b2: The sandwich sign describes mesenteric vessels and fat being encased by enlarged lymph nodes, a classic appearance of abdominal lymphadenopathy. Think of nodes as the “bread” surrounding the central mesentery “filling.”
chest-b3: Abdominal lymph nodes are generally considered abnormal when they measure more than 10 mm. A good memory tip: 1 cm is the common cutoff for pathologic nodal enlargement.
chest-b4: Fluid around the lungs is called a pleural effusion because it collects in the pleural space. Remember: pleural = lung lining, while pericardial = heart lining.
chest-b5: In hemophiliac patients, the psoas muscle is the most common site of retroperitoneal hematoma. Remember: spontaneous bleeding often tracks into deep muscles, especially the psoas.
chest-b6: Lung consolidation occurs when normally air-filled alveoli are replaced by fluid, pus, blood, or cells. Key fact: consolidated lung may appear tissue-like on ultrasound, similar to the liver.
chest-b7: Free air in the pleural space outside the lung is a pneumothorax. Remember: “pneumo” means air and “thorax” refers to the chest.
chest-b8: Pulmonary sequestration is nonfunctioning lung tissue that is separate from the normal bronchial tree and has its own blood supply. Key memory point: it often receives systemic arterial flow, commonly from the aorta.
chest-b9: Cystic adenomatoid malformation is a fetal developmental mass made of abnormal bronchial and lung tissue. Remember: it is a congenital lung lesion detected prenatally in the fetal chest.
chest-b10: Thoracentesis is the procedure used to remove fluid from the pleural space for diagnosis or treatment. Memory tip: thorax = chest, so thoracentesis targets chest fluid.
chest-b11: Hematomas can appear hyperechoic, hypoechoic, or complex depending on their age and stage of organization. Key fact: blood changes sonographic appearance over time, so hematomas are variable.
chest-b12: Fluid around the heart is termed a pericardial effusion because it collects within the pericardial sac. Remember: peri- means around, and cardial refers to the heart.
chest-b13: Retroperitoneal fibrosis most commonly appears as a hypoechoic mass surrounding the aorta. Key fact: it often extends around nearby structures and may entrap the ureters, causing obstruction.
chest-b14: Weight loss is not a typical clinical finding of retroperitoneal hematoma, whereas trauma, hemophilia, and low hematocrit are common clues. Remember: hematoma usually presents with bleeding-related symptoms, not chronic constitutional signs.
chest-b15: Enlargement of abdominal lymph nodes is called retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Memory tip: adenopathy means gland or lymph node disease/enlargement.
neck-b16: Graves disease is the most likely diagnosis because hyperthyroidism with exophthalmos (bulging eyes) is classic for Graves. Remember: Graves often causes a diffusely enlarged, hypervascular thyroid on ultrasound.
neck-b17: Colloid is the fluid within thyroid follicles that stores thyroid hormone precursors. Remember: colloid fills the follicles and serves as the thyroid’s hormone reservoir.
neck-b18: Hashimoto thyroiditis commonly leads to hypothyroidism, meaning the gland produces too few thyroid hormones. Remember: Hashimoto is an autoimmune process that gradually destroys normal thyroid tissue.
neck-b19: The thyroid requires iodine to synthesize T3 and T4 hormones. Remember: without adequate iodine, normal thyroid hormone production cannot occur.
neck-b20: The longus colli muscles lie posterior to each thyroid lobe and are important posterior landmarks on thyroid ultrasound. Remember: posterior thyroid pathology is often assessed relative to the longus colli.
neck-b21: The sternocleidomastoid muscles are located lateral to the thyroid lobes and are a key lateral neck landmark. Remember: the carotid artery and jugular vein also lie deep to the SCM.
neck-b22: The esophagus can mimic a posterior left thyroid or parathyroid mass because it lies just behind the left thyroid lobe near the trachea. Remember: swallowing or seeing air may help identify it as esophagus.
neck-b23: The internal carotid artery is the vascular structure identified as closest to the thyroid lobes in this question set. Remember: carotid artery anatomy is an important lateral landmark during thyroid scanning.
neck-b24: An isthmus measuring greater than 10 mm suggests thyroid enlargement. Remember: the isthmus is normally thin, so marked thickening raises concern for diffuse goiter.
neck-b25: The strap muscles lie anterior to the thyroid gland and commonly appear as thin hypoechoic muscles on ultrasound. Remember: sternohyoid and sternothyroid are part of the strap muscle group.
neck-b26: The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid artery. Remember: it supplies the upper thyroid pole and is a useful Doppler landmark.
neck-b27: Iodine is not a thyroid hormone; it is a raw material the gland uses to make hormones. Remember: the thyroid produces T4, T3, and calcitonin.
neck-b28: Thyroxine (T4) is the most abundantly produced thyroid hormone. Remember: although T3 is more active, the thyroid releases much more T4.
neck-b29: The thyroid is an endocrine gland because it secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream. Remember: endocrine glands are ductless, unlike exocrine glands.
neck-b30: The pyramidal lobe is the superior extension of the thyroid isthmus. Remember: it is a normal variant and represents a remnant related to thyroid embryologic descent.
chest-b16: Pulmonary sequestration is a congenital mass of nonfunctioning lung tissue, not a typical cause of acquired lung consolidation. Remember: consolidation usually comes from alveoli filling with fluid, pus, blood, or tumor cells.
chest-b17: Pneumothorax is a known post-thoracentesis complication and is commonly confirmed with chest radiography. Key memory aid: introducing a needle into the pleural space can accidentally let air enter it.
chest-b18: Pneumothorax is the most common significant complication after thoracentesis because the pleura and lung can be inadvertently punctured. Remember: air in the pleural space after a chest procedure is the classic concern.
chest-b19: Abdominal lymph nodes are commonly found in the mesentery, renal hilum, and para-aortic region, not typically within the subhepatic space. Remember: abdominal nodal chains usually track along vessels and mesentery.
chest-b20: Lung consolidation often shows branching linear internal echoes from air within bronchi, known as air bronchograms. Key fact: consolidated lung can look tissue-like, but the bright branching bronchi help identify it.
chest-b21: Multiple hypoechoic masses along the anterior border of the abdominal aorta are classic for retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Remember: enlarged para-aortic nodes often appear as clustered masses following the great vessels.
chest-b22: Retroperitoneal fibrosis can present as a large hypoechoic abdominal mass and is associated with certain drugs, including migraine medications. Key memory aid: it often forms plaque-like soft tissue in the retroperitoneum.
chest-b23: Abnormal lymph nodes are typically enlarged, often greater than 1 cm, so 'less than 1 cm' is the false statement. Remember: malignant or infected nodes commonly lose the echogenic hilum and become rounder.
chest-b24: An anechoic triangular fluid collection superior to the right hemidiaphragm is most consistent with pleural effusion. Key fact: pleural fluid often collects dependently above the diaphragm and may be seen during RUQ scanning.
chest-b25: Hematocrit helps assess for active bleeding because it reflects the proportion of red blood cells in blood. Remember: after a femoral artery puncture, falling hematocrit can suggest hemorrhage or retroperitoneal bleed.
chest-b26: Infected pleural effusions can have variable appearances and may be anechoic, complex, or septated. Key memory aid: empyemas often become more complex as inflammatory debris and fibrin strands develop.
chest-b27: Hemophilia is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of clotting factors, leading to impaired blood clotting. Remember: hemophiliacs bleed longer because the coagulation cascade is defective, not because platelets are high.
chest-b28: Consolidated lung often becomes 'hepatized,' meaning it appears tissue-like and isoechoic to the liver. Key fact: this liver-like appearance is a classic ultrasound clue for lung consolidation.
chest-b29: Enlarged lymph nodes commonly become more hypoechoic and may even appear nearly anechoic compared with normal nodes. Remember: as nodes become abnormal, they often lose their bright fatty hilum and darken.
chest-b30: Bronchial infections are generally not discovered sonographically because normal aerated lung blocks ultrasound transmission. Remember: ultrasound is best for pleural, peripheral lung, and mediastinal-adjacent abnormalities, not air-filled bronchi.
neck-b1: Thyroglossal duct cysts are congenital midline neck cysts classically found near the hyoid bone, often superior to the thyroid. Remember: thyroglossal cyst = midline; branchial cleft cyst = lateral neck.
neck-b2: The adult neck normally has four parathyroid glands, usually two superior and two inferior. A helpful memory: parathyroid glands commonly come in pairs on each side of the thyroid.
neck-b3: A branchial cleft cyst typically appears as a lateral neck cystic mass near the mandibular angle. Remember: branchial cleft lesions are lateral, while thyroglossal duct cysts are usually midline.
neck-b4: A cold nodule is nonfunctioning on nuclear imaging and has a higher risk of malignancy than a hot nodule. Key fact: hot nodules are usually hyperfunctioning and more often benign.
neck-b5: Parathyroid glands regulate calcium balance through parathyroid hormone, affecting calcium release, absorption, and reabsorption. Remember: parathyroid = PTH = phosphate and calcium control, not thyroid hormone production.
neck-b6: A normal cervical lymph node typically should not measure greater than 10 mm in short-axis size. Key fact: benign nodes are usually small, oval, and maintain an echogenic hilum.
neck-b7: Parathyroid adenomas commonly cause primary hyperparathyroidism, which leads to elevated serum calcium levels. Remember: too much PTH raises calcium by acting on bone, kidneys, and intestines.
neck-b8: A normal cervical lymph node is usually hypoechoic, oval or oblong, and contains a central echogenic hilum. Memory tip: benign nodes keep their hilum and elongated shape.
neck-b9: Graves disease produces the classic thyroid inferno, meaning markedly increased diffuse thyroid vascularity on Doppler. Remember: inferno = hypervascular diffuse toxic goiter, a hallmark of Graves.
neck-b10: Malignant thyroid nodules are more often hypoechoic rather than echogenic, so an echogenic mass is the exception listed here. Key fact: calcifications, nodal spread, and a solitary suspicious nodule raise concern for cancer.
neck-b11: A cold nodule is not a benign diagnostic feature because nonfunctioning nodules carry greater malignant potential. Remember: benign clues include cystic appearance, eggshell calcification, and hyperechogenicity.
neck-b12: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer and often spreads to cervical lymph nodes. Key fact: papillary thyroid cancer generally has a favorable prognosis despite nodal metastases.
neck-b13: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism due to autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue. Remember: Hashimoto often causes an enlarged heterogeneous gland early, then decreased thyroid function.
neck-b14: An echogenic hilum is a normal lymph node feature, so it is the exception among abnormal findings. Key fact: abnormal nodes tend to become round, enlarged, and may lose the fatty hilum.
neck-b15: Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism and classically causes diffuse gland enlargement with hypervascularity. Remember: Graves = overactive thyroid + thyroid inferno on Doppler.
male-b1: Seminoma is the most common primary testicular malignancy, especially in young adult men. Remember: seminomas are classic germ cell tumors and are often more radiosensitive than nonseminomatous tumors.
male-b2: Secondary varicoceles suggest an underlying obstructing process, so they are more concerning when right-sided or associated with a renal/retroperitoneal mass. Remember: a typical primary varicocele is usually left-sided.
male-b3: Benign prostatic hypertrophy most commonly arises in the transitional zone, which surrounds the proximal urethra. Remember: this location explains why BPH often causes urinary outlet obstruction symptoms.
male-b4: In older men, prostate enlargement is most often due to benign prostatic hypertrophy rather than cancer or infection. Remember: BPH is extremely common with aging and usually affects the transitional zone.
male-b5: A spermatocele is a benign cystic lesion usually located in the epididymal head and may contain low-level internal echoes from sperm or debris. Remember: epididymal head plus debris strongly suggests spermatocele.
male-b6: A varicocele is an abnormal dilation of the pampiniform plexus veins within the scrotum. Remember: on ultrasound it often appears as multiple serpiginous vessels that enlarge with Valsalva.
male-b7: Primary varicoceles are commonly left-sided and may present as a palpable extratesticular mass or be linked to infertility. Remember: retroperitoneal mass suggests a secondary, not primary, varicocele.
male-b8: A spermatocele is the common cystic lesion in the epididymal head that contains nonviable sperm. Remember: spermatocele = sperm-containing cyst, usually arising from the epididymal head.
male-b9: Incompetent valves in the pampiniform plexus cause venous dilation known as a varicocele. Remember: varicoceles are classically described as feeling like a 'bag of worms.'
male-b10: The blue dot sign is classic for torsion of the testicular appendage, representing the ischemic appendage seen through the scrotal skin. Remember: this condition usually preserves normal intratesticular blood flow.
male-b11: Varicocele is strongly associated with male infertility because venous stasis and increased scrotal temperature can impair spermatogenesis. Remember: it is a common and often correctable infertility factor.
male-b12: Torsion of the testicular appendage usually has preserved intratesticular blood flow, so absent intratesticular flow suggests testicular torsion instead. Remember: appendage torsion causes a focal adjacent lesion, not global testicular ischemia.
male-b13: Varicocele is the most common correctable cause of male infertility. Remember: treatment can improve fertility because the problem is often due to reversible venous congestion and heat stress.
male-b14: A hydrocele is a simple fluid collection surrounding the testis, usually within the tunica vaginalis. Remember: uncomplicated hydroceles are anechoic and can transilluminate clinically.
male-b15: The exocrine function of the testes is sperm production within the seminiferous tubules. Remember: testosterone is the endocrine product, while sperm is the exocrine product.
male-b16: A hydrocele most commonly collects as fluid between the visceral and parietal layers of the tunica vaginalis. Remember: it is the most common cause of painless scrotal enlargement.
male-b17: Testicular torsion typically causes sudden, severe testicular pain that often begins at rest and is a surgical emergency. Key fact: salvage rates drop sharply after about 6 hours of ischemia.
male-b18: In a child with acute focal pain at the superior pole of the testis, torsion of the testicular appendage is most likely. Remember the classic clue: the painful superior pole may show a 'blue dot' sign.
male-b19: A varicocele is diagnosed when pampiniform plexus veins measure greater than 2 mm, especially if they enlarge with Valsalva. Key fact: these dilated veins often look like a 'bag of worms.'
male-b20: Bell-clapper deformity means the testis lacks normal posterior fixation, allowing it to swing freely and predisposing to torsion. Remember: this congenital abnormality is a major risk factor for intravaginal torsion.
male-b21: The Valsalva maneuver increases venous pressure and can accentuate reflux and venous dilation, making a varicocele easier to detect sonographically. Key fact: varicoceles often become more apparent with standing plus Valsalva.
male-b22: The testes' endocrine function is testosterone production, primarily by the Leydig cells. Remember: seminiferous tubules make sperm, while Leydig cells make testosterone.
male-b23: Hyperemic intratesticular flow is not typical of testicular torsion; torsion usually shows decreased or absent flow compared with the normal side. Remember: hyperemia is more characteristic of epididymitis-orchitis.
male-b24: Spermatogenesis takes place in the seminiferous tubules within the testes. Key fact: sperm then drain toward the rete testis after being produced in these tubules.
male-b25: Cryptorchidism means one or both testes have failed to descend into the scrotum. Remember: an undescended testis has increased risks of infertility and malignancy.
male-b26: Seminoma is the most common germ cell tumor of the testis overall. Key fact: it often presents as a homogeneous hypoechoic intratesticular mass in men ages 30-40.
male-b27: Varicoceles occur most commonly on the left because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, increasing venous pressure. Remember: isolated right-sided varicocele is less common and may need further evaluation.
male-b28: Most prostatic cancers arise in the peripheral zone, which is also the area commonly sampled and palpated on rectal exam. Remember: benign prostatic hyperplasia usually affects the transitional zone instead.
