male-b29: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer found in men. Key fact: it is highly prevalent, especially with increasing age, though not all cases are clinically aggressive.
male-b30: A seminoma most commonly appears as a hypoechoic testicular mass on ultrasound. Remember: seminomas are often more homogeneous than nonseminomatous germ cell tumors.
msk-b1: Cellulitis is an infection/inflammation of the skin and subcutaneous soft tissues. Remember: on ultrasound it often appears as diffuse subcutaneous edema with a classic “cobblestone” pattern.
msk-b2: Tendonitis typically causes pain, swelling, and warmth from inflammation, not itching. A good memory aid: inflamed tendons act like other inflamed tissues—think pain, heat, and edema.
msk-b3: The Thompson test helps detect an Achilles tendon tear by squeezing the calf and observing for plantarflexion. Key fact: absent plantarflexion strongly suggests Achilles rupture.
msk-b4: A cystic mass in the popliteal fossa is classically a Baker cyst. Remember: Baker cysts arise behind the knee, often between the semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius.
msk-b5: A ganglion cyst is a very common cystic mass along the dorsal wrist or hand. Memory tip: ganglion cysts are the classic “dorsal wrist lump.”
msk-b6: The Achilles tendon attaches the calf muscles to the calcaneus, so it connects the calf muscle to the heel. Key fact: it is the strongest and thickest tendon in the body.
msk-b7: Prone positioning gives the best access to the posterior ankle for Achilles tendon evaluation. Remember: posterior structures of the lower leg are usually scanned best with the patient prone.
msk-b8: In the Thompson test, the patient lies prone while the examiner squeezes the symptomatic calf. Key fact: a normal Achilles tendon causes plantarflexion when the calf is compressed.
msk-b9: Lipomas are benign fatty tumors that are usually painless. Remember: a soft, mobile, nonpainful mass is a classic presentation of a lipoma.
msk-b10: Foreign bodies are usually echogenic, not hypoechoic, so that statement is the exception. Key fact: metallic foreign bodies often produce comet-tail or reverberation artifact.
msk-b11: A lipoma is a benign tumor made of adipose tissue. Memory aid: “lipo-” refers to fat, making lipoma the classic benign fatty mass.
msk-b12: A hemangioma is a benign tumor composed of blood vessels. Remember: “heman-” refers to blood, so hemangioma means a vascular lesion.
msk-b13: A high-frequency linear-array transducer is best for a hand splinter because superficial structures need high resolution. Key fact: linear probes provide excellent near-field detail for soft-tissue foreign bodies.
msk-b14: A Baker cyst forms from synovial fluid distending a weakened knee joint capsule, often with arthritis. Remember: it is the classic fluid collection behind the knee.
msk-b15: Fluid in the synovial sheath indicates tendosynovitis, which is inflammation of a tendon sheath. Key fact: sonography may show sheath fluid and sometimes hyperemia on Doppler.
msk-b16: Refractive shadowing occurs when the sound beam bends at the edge of a curved structure, creating an edge shadow distal to it. Remember: refraction = beam bending, most often seen at curved margins.
msk-b17: Tendosynovitis means inflammation of both the tendon and its synovial sheath. Memory tip: “teno-” refers to tendon and “synovitis” refers to the inflamed sheath lining.
msk-b18: A complicated Baker cyst may contain internal pannus, seen as a thin flap-like tissue projection. Remember: pannus represents inflamed synovial tissue and can make a simple cyst look complex.
msk-b19: A Baker cyst can cause calf pain and swelling that clinically resembles deep venous thrombosis. Key fact: a ruptured Baker cyst especially can mimic DVT symptoms.
msk-b20: Normal muscle is relatively hypoechoic with linear echogenic fibroadipose septa running through it. Think: muscle looks dark overall, crossed by bright parallel strands.
msk-b21: Ganglion cysts are most commonly found along the dorsal, not anterior, aspect of the wrist and hand. Remember: classic ganglion location is the dorsal wrist between the carpals.
msk-b22: A partial tendon tear usually appears as a focal hypoechoic defect within the normally echogenic tendon fibers. Key memory point: torn tendon fibers lose their bright fibrillar pattern.
msk-b23: Tendons are echogenic, fibrous structures that connect muscle to bone. Remember: ligaments connect bone to bone, while tendons transmit muscle force to bone.
msk-b24: A standoff pad improves visualization of very superficial structures by moving them into the transducer’s focal zone. Think: standoff pads are for near-field detail, not deep anatomy.
msk-b25: Hyperemic flow on Doppler usually indicates inflammation because inflamed tissues recruit increased blood supply. Memory aid: “hot” inflamed tissue tends to look vascular.
msk-b26: Supine with the knee flexed is not the standard position for Achilles tendon assessment. Best practice is prone with the feet hanging off the bed to fully evaluate the tendon.
msk-b27: A negative Thompson test means squeezing the calf causes plantarflexion, indicating the Achilles tendon is still functionally intact. Remember: absent plantarflexion suggests complete rupture.
msk-b28: Superficial lipomas may be hypo-, iso-, or hyperechoic relative to surrounding tissue, but they are not typically anechoic. Key fact: anechoic masses suggest simple fluid, not fat.
msk-b29: Metallic foreign bodies commonly create comet-tail artifact from reverberation between highly reflective surfaces. Remember: bright metal often produces a dirty trailing echo pattern.
msk-b30: Air at the site of a foreign body can generate bright echoes and obscure the true orientation of the object. Memory tip: air is a strong reflector and often complicates localization.
